..After an active day, weather remains active across 
portions of Utah this evening. This is to an extent the result of
a deepening PacNW trough helping to strengthen a Pacific moisture
tap within the associated enhanced southwesterly flow. To that 
end, mesoanalysis maintains widespread PWAT values in excess of 1"
across the majority of Utah, or around 150-200% of climatological
normal for late August. Further, the aforementioned deepening 
PacNW trough has allowed a frontal boundary to slowly advance into
northern Utah, and the abnormally strong deep layer flow overhead
has allowed for impressive effective shear on the order of 40-60 
kts across the northern half of Utah, and around 20-40 kts across 
southern Utah. This anomalous combination of ingredients has 
yielded numerous strong to severe thunderstorms with strong winds 
and hail, and heavy rain resulting in multiple instances of flash 
flooding.

Looking ahead to the overnight hours, while overall instability 
will decrease with the lack of sun, enough will remain in 
combination with ample moisture to result in continued showers and
thunderstorms. In general, anticipate these to tend to be weaker 
than those during the daytime Saturday. That said, wouldn't rule 
out one or two pulsing up at times, and with the moisture rich 
environment, any stronger Storm or training storm impacting a rain
sensitive basin in particular could pose a flash flood threat. In
terms of coverage, models largely support the bulk of the 
scattered activity across portions of central Utah, in the rough 
vicinity near and to the south of the frontal boundary.

Sunday appears to have potential to be another active day capable
of strong storms and flash flooding. In terms of the broader 
synoptic environment, the ingredients don't appear to change 
significantly, with an embedded midlevel shortwave impulse also 
shifting through. Strong flow will remain overhead allowing 
moisture will continue to advect into the region. One difference 
is it appears some slightly drier air will start to shift into 
Utah from the west, with the best available moisture becoming 
positioned across eastern Utah to southwest Wyoming, generally 
along/east of the I-15 corridor and south of I-80. As such, this 
area is highlighted as Slight Risk (categorical 2/4) for excessive
rainfall from WPC, and much of it is also included in a Flood 
Watch for potential flash flooding. Elsewhere across all but far 
west to northwest Utah, a Marginal Risk (categorical 1/4) of 
excessive rainfall is noted. These areas will need to remain 
weather aware for strong storms capable of periods of heavy 
rainfall once again, with flash flooding especially possible in 
those typically sensitive basins (recent burn scars, slot canyons,
typically dry washes, and slickrock areas). One possible 
difference is that shear appears to be maybe around 20 kts or so 
weaker than Saturday, which may limit the coverage of strong to 
severe storms. Still, would anticipate a few organized storms will
still be capable of strong gusty winds and hail.

Monday will yet again see the potential for flash flooding and 
strong storms. Overall, the synoptic elements once again do not 
shift significantly, and another shortwave impulse will lift 
through overhead during the day. Like Sunday, the expectation is 
that while strong to maybe a few severe storms will certainly be 
possible, the moisture rich environment will favor flash flooding 
as the primary risk. As far as the excessive rainfall outlook, the
slight and marginal risk areas change very little from that of 
Sunday, and thus the same areas will remain more favored for the 
threat. With multiple days of repeat thunderstorms, saturated 
soils and any remaining high creeks/rivers/etc. may further 
exacerbate this potential.

The deep PacNW trough will more or less maintain its position 
Tuesday onward through the upcoming week, but the moisture tap 
will become less defined. As such, a general drying trend is 
expected across the forecast region, and the threat of widespread 
heavy rainfall generally appears lower. Still, the PacNW trough 
will offer potential for some grazing shortwaves, and there will 
still be enough moisture lingering to result in the development of
some showers and thunderstorms day to day. Even if the threat of 
widespread heavy rain may be lower, any stronger or slower moving 
storm that gets over a rain sensitive basin will pose a risk, so 
cannot say the threat is zero. Overall though, there is some 
uncertainty noted in the day to day specifics.

Though on the tail end of the forecast range, next weekend bears 
at least some watching. Deterministic models show potential for 
the Pacific moisture tap to become reestablished, with ensembles
